parts.title: The 200 dollar storage unit - part 1
parts.story: No shot. That's exactly what I said out loud when I won an abandoned storage unit at auction for two hundred dollars and rolled up the door. Most of it was what you'd expect, broken furniture, boxes of old clothes, a rusted bike. But pushed into the very back corner, under a tarp, was an antique trunk with a heavy iron lock and initials carved into the top that were worn almost smooth. The auctioneer told me units like this are usually junk, that nobody leaves anything valuable behind. But nobody locks a trunk with a lock like that for no reason, and nobody shoves it in the back under a tarp unless they're hiding it. I loaded it into my truck, drove home, and stared at it in my garage for an hour before I got the bolt cutters. What was inside when that lock finally snapped open didn't look valuable at all. It looked personal. Part 2 is on my profile.
parts.caption: I paid $200 for an abandoned storage unit 👀 follow for part 2

parts.title: The 200 dollar storage unit - part 2
parts.story: It's giving haunted. That was my first thought when the trunk from the storage unit finally popped open. Inside wasn't gold or cash, it was someone's entire life. A folded military uniform, a stack of letters tied with faded ribbon, black and white photos of a young couple, and a child's tiny shoe wrapped in tissue paper. At the very bottom was a sealed envelope, yellowed with age, with four words written across it in shaky handwriting: do not open yet. Now I've watched enough movies to know you don't ignore a message like that. But I also couldn't just leave it. So I read the letters first, hoping they'd tell me who these people were. They did. And halfway through the third letter, I realized this trunk wasn't abandoned by accident. Someone had been forced to leave it behind, and the last letter explained exactly why in a way that made my stomach drop. Part 3 is on my profile.
parts.caption: There was a sealed envelope that said DO NOT OPEN 😳 follow for part 3

parts.title: The 200 dollar storage unit - part 3
parts.story: Red flag. The whole thing was one big red flag once I read the letters in that trunk. They were between a soldier named Thomas and a woman named Margaret, written in the nineteen sixties, full of plans for a life together. But the last letter wasn't from either of them. It was from a lawyer, dated much later, and it mentioned a property, a house, that legally still belonged to the family and had never been sold. It listed an address forty minutes from where I live. Here's the red flag that made me pause: the storage unit had been rented under a completely different name than anyone in those letters. Someone had put this trunk into storage decades after these people would have been gone, and then just stopped paying, letting it get auctioned off to a stranger. To me. Why would someone hide a family's entire history in a locked trunk and then abandon it? I decided to drive to that address and find out. Part 4 is on my profile.
parts.caption: The address was 40 minutes from my house 🚗 follow for part 4

parts.title: The 200 dollar storage unit - part 4
parts.story: Delulu. I felt completely delulu driving to a stranger's house holding a trunk full of someone else's memories, rehearsing what I'd even say. The address was a small brick house with a garden out front. I knocked, and an older woman answered. I told her I'd bought a storage unit and found a trunk with letters mentioning this address, and I asked if the names Thomas and Margaret meant anything to her. She went completely still. Her hand went to her mouth. Then she said Margaret was her mother, that Thomas died overseas before she was born, and that after her mother passed, her own brother had cleared out the house and sold everything, telling her nothing was left. That trunk, she said, held the only photos of her parents that ever existed. Photos she thought were gone forever. She started crying on the porch, and then she asked me one question I wasn't ready for. Part 5 is on my profile.
parts.caption: She said the photos were her parents she thought were gone forever 😭 follow for part 5

parts.title: The 200 dollar storage unit - part 5
parts.story: Big W. Here's how the storage unit story ended, and it's a big W for everyone. The woman on the porch, Margaret's daughter, asked me how much I wanted for the trunk, already reaching for her purse with shaking hands. I told her the truth, that I paid two hundred dollars for the whole unit and I would never in a million years sell her family back to her. I just wanted her to have it. She hugged me on that porch like she'd known me her whole life. It turned out her brother had hidden the trunk in storage out of spite after a family fight, then died himself, and the unit got abandoned and auctioned to me by pure chance. She invited me in, made coffee, and showed me a wall of family photos she could finally complete. I gained a friend that day, and she gained her parents back. Follow me, because the next story is about a letter I found that led somewhere even crazier.
parts.caption: I gave her the trunk for free 🥹 the whole story is on my page
